title: Neovim
subtitle: modes, motions, operators and the editing grammar

levels.title: Modes & Survival
levels.goal: Know which mode you are in, and how to get back to Normal.
levels.brief:
Vim's one big idea: **your keyboard means different things in different
modes.** Most editors have one mode — every key inserts a character. Vim has
several, and *Normal* is home.

| Mode | You get there by | Keys mean |
|---|---|---|
| **Normal** | `Esc` (always) | commands |
| **Insert** | `i` `a` `o` `I` `A` `O` | literal text |
| **Visual** | `v` `V` `Ctrl-v` | select |
| **Command-line** | `:` `/` `?` | ex commands / search |

**The habit that matters most: return to Normal the moment you stop typing.**
Not when you need a command — immediately. Normal mode is the resting position,
the way the home row is the resting position for your fingers.

Movement in Normal mode is `h j k l`:

```
      k        h  ←  left
 h  <   >  l   j  ↓  down
      j        k  ↑  up
                l  →  right
```

Yes, arrow keys work. Use `hjkl` anyway — they are under your fingers, and
every operator in Vim composes with them.

lessons.title: Left and right
lessons.teach: Move the cursor onto the `w` of `world` using only `l`.
lessons.hint: Six presses of `l`. Count the characters — `hello ` is six.

lessons.title: Down and up
lessons.teach: `j` goes down, `k` goes up. Get to the last line.
lessons.hint: `j` twice.

lessons.title: Navigate a small function
lessons.teach: Put the cursor on the `p` of `print` (line 2, column 4).
lessons.hint: Down once, then right four times.

lessons.title: Insert before the cursor
lessons.teach: `i` enters Insert mode **before** the cursor. Type the missing word, then press `Esc`. Never leave a lesson in Insert mode.
lessons.hint: `i` then `mundo` then `Esc`.

lessons.title: Append after the cursor
lessons.teach: `a` enters Insert **after** the cursor. This is the difference that trips up every beginner: at the end of a line, `i` cannot reach the last position — `a` can.
lessons.hint: The cursor is on `)`. `a` puts you just past it.

lessons.title: Escape from a mistake
lessons.teach: You are going to make a mess and then undo it. Type `xyz`, press `Esc`, then press `u` to undo. Vim's undo is per *insertion*, not per keystroke — the whole `xyz` disappears at once.

lessons.title: Which mode?
lessons.teach: A quick check before moving on.
lessons.question: You just pressed `Esc`, then `d`, and nothing seems to have happened. What is Vim waiting for?
options: Nothing — `d` did nothing and was discarded
A motion or text object to tell `d` what to delete
lessons.why: `d` is an *operator*. It is incomplete on its own and waits for a motion (`dw`, `d$`) or a doubled key (`dd`). This pending state is the heart of Vim's grammar — Level 3 is built on it. `Esc` cancels it.

links.note: hjkl are home-row keys — Typing Level 2 drills exactly this cluster.

levels.title: Efficient Motions
levels.brief:
`hjkl` is for fine adjustment. Real navigation happens in words and lines.

**Within a line**

| Key | Moves to |
|---|---|
| `w` | start of next **word** (punctuation counts as a word) |
| `W` | start of next **WORD** (whitespace-delimited only) |
| `b` | back to start of word |
| `e` | end of current/next word |
| `0` | column 0 |
| `^` | first non-blank character |
| `$` | end of line |

`word` vs `WORD` matters constantly in code: in `self.items[0]`, `w` stops at
`.`, `items`, `[`, `0`, `]` — five stops. `W` treats the whole thing as one.

**Across the file**

| Key | Moves to |
|---|---|
| `gg` | first line |
| `G` | last line |
| `{n}G` | line n (also `:{n}`) |
| `{` `}` | previous / next blank line |

**Counts.** Almost every motion takes a count prefix: `3w` = three words forward,
`5j` = five lines down. `count + motion` is the first half of Vim's grammar.

lessons.title: Word by word
lessons.teach: Get to `three` with word motions, not `l`.
lessons.hint: `w` twice.

lessons.title: Counted words
lessons.teach: Same idea, with a count. Land on `four`.
lessons.hint: `3w` — one keystroke cheaper than `www`.

lessons.title: End of word
lessons.teach: `e` lands on the *last* character of a word. Get to the `e` of `three`.

lessons.title: Backwards
lessons.teach: From the end, walk back to `two`.

lessons.title: word vs WORD
lessons.teach: `self.items[0]` is five *words* but one **WORD**. `E` jumps to the end of the WORD; lowercase `e` would need five presses to get there.
lessons.hint: `E` — the WORD version of `e`.

lessons.title: Line ends
lessons.teach: `$` goes to the last character; `^` to the first non-blank. Get to the closing brace.

lessons.title: First non-blank
lessons.teach: The cursor is at the end. `0` would put you in the indentation; `^` puts you on real content.

lessons.title: Top and bottom
lessons.teach: Jump to the last line, then to line 3.
lessons.hint: `G` then `3G`. `3G` alone would also do it — but practise both.

lessons.title: Paragraph hops
lessons.teach: `}` jumps to the next blank line. Get from the first function to the second.
lessons.hint: `}` lands on the blank line; then `j`.

links.note: The buffers you navigate here are the Python constructs of Level 2.

levels.title: The Grammar: Operator + Motion
levels.goal: Learn one rule, get a hundred commands for free.
levels.brief:
This is the level that turns Vim from "a weird editor" into a language.

```
   [count]  operator  [count]  motion
      2        d                w        →  delete two words
               c                $        →  change to end of line
      3        y                y        →  yank three lines
```

**Operators**

| Op | Does |
|---|---|
| `d` | delete (into a register — it is a *cut*, not a discard) |
| `c` | change = delete, then enter Insert mode |
| `y` | yank (copy) |
| `>` `<` | indent / outdent |
| `gu` `gU` | lowercase / uppercase |

**Doubling an operator makes it act on whole lines**: `dd`, `cc`, `yy`, `>>`.

You already know a dozen motions from Level 2. Multiply: `dw` `d$` `d0` `dG`
`dgg` `d}` `cw` `c$` `ce` `yw` `y$` `yG` `>}` `gUw`… none of these had to be
memorised separately. That is the whole point.

**`c` deletes slightly differently from `d`.** `cw` behaves like `ce` — it
changes to the *end* of the word, not up to the next one, because deleting the
trailing space before typing a replacement is almost never what you want.

lessons.title: Delete a word
lessons.teach: `dw` deletes from the cursor to the start of the next word.
lessons.hint: Cursor is on `t` of `this`.

lessons.title: Delete to end of line
lessons.teach: `d$` — or its synonym `D`.

lines: keep this # delete this trailing comment

lessons.hint: `d$`, cursor already on `#`.

lessons.title: Change a word
lessons.teach: `cw` deletes the word and drops you in Insert mode. Replace `foo` with `bar`, then `Esc`.

lessons.title: Delete a line
lessons.teach: `dd`. The line is gone and the register holds it.

lessons.title: Counted line delete
lessons.teach: `3dd` removes three lines. Delete the whole body of the function.
lessons.hint: `3dd` from line 2.

lessons.title: Delete to end of file
lessons.teach: `dG` deletes from the current line to the last line. Truncate the file after the docstring.

lessons.title: Change to end of line
lessons.teach: `C` is `c$`. Replace the whole return expression.
lessons.hint: Cursor sits on `o` of `old_value`.

lessons.title: Indent a block
lessons.teach: `>` with a motion, or `>>` for one line. Indent both body lines by one level using a count.
lessons.hint: `2>>` — the count goes before the doubled operator.

lessons.title: Uppercase a word
lessons.teach: `gU` + motion. Turn the constant name into SCREAMING_CASE.
lessons.hint: `gUe` — uppercase to end of word. `e` because `_` is a word character.

lessons.title: Compose it yourself
lessons.teach: You have the grammar now. Use it.
lessons.question: The cursor is at the start of a 40-line function. You want to delete the function and copy nothing. Which is the cheapest correct command?
lessons.why: `d}` deletes to the next blank line — no counting required, and it adapts if the function is 38 or 44 lines. `40dd` needs you to count; `dG` deletes the rest of the file. `"_d}` also works and additionally avoids clobbering the register (Level 7).

links.note: Typing Level 11 drills these exact sequences as text.

levels.title: Entering Insert Mode Well
levels.goal: Six doors into Insert mode. Pick the right one.
levels.brief:
Beginners use `i` for everything and then navigate inside Insert mode with
arrow keys. That is the slow path. Choose the entry point that lands the cursor
where you want it:

| Key | Enters Insert… |
|---|---|
| `i` | before the cursor |
| `a` | after the cursor |
| `I` | at the first non-blank of the line |
| `A` | at the end of the line |
| `o` | on a new line **below** |
| `O` | on a new line **above** |
| `s` | deleting the character under the cursor |
| `S` / `cc` | deleting the whole line's content, keeping indent |

`A` and `o` are the two you will use most: appending to a line and opening a new
one are what writing code actually consists of.

**Inside Insert mode, do as little as possible.** No arrow keys, no mouse. Type
the text, press `Esc`, move in Normal mode. Every excursion inside Insert mode is
a change Vim cannot repeat with `.` (Level 8).

lessons.title: Append at end of line
lessons.teach: `A` — the single most useful insert command. Add the missing colon.

lessons.title: Insert at first non-blank
lessons.teach: `I` ignores indentation. Comment out the line.
lessons.hint: `I` then `# ` then `Esc`.

lessons.title: Open a line below
lessons.teach: `o` from anywhere on the line.

lessons.title: Open a line above
lessons.teach: `O`. Add the shebang.

lessons.title: Substitute one character
lessons.teach: `s` deletes the character under the cursor and inserts. Fix the operator.
lessons.hint: Cursor is on `=`. `s` then `==`.

lessons.title: Replace the whole line
lessons.teach: `S` (or `cc`) clears the line but keeps its indentation.

lessons.title: o keeps indentation
lessons.teach: Notice that `o` inherits the current line's indent — you do not type the spaces. Add a second statement to the body.

lessons.title: A vs i at end of line
lessons.teach: One of Vim's genuine gotchas.
lessons.question: The cursor is on the final `)` of `foo()` and you want to type `:` after it. `i:` gives you `foo(:)`. Why?
options: `i` is broken at end of line
`i` inserts *before* the cursor, and the cursor is on `)`, not past it
You need to be in Replace mode
lessons.why: In Normal mode the cursor sits *on* a character, never between two. `i` inserts to its left. To get to the right of the last character you need `a` — or `A`, which goes to the end of the line regardless of where you are.

levels.title: Find & Till: Surgical Line Motions
levels.goal: f F t T ; , — the fastest way to a character.
levels.brief:
`f{char}` jumps **onto** the next occurrence of `{char}` on the current line.
`t{char}` stops **till** just before it. Capitals search backwards.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `f,` | forward onto the next `,` |
| `F,` | backward onto the previous `,` |
| `t)` | forward, stopping before `)` |
| `T(` | backward, stopping after `(` |
| `;` | repeat the last f/F/t/T |
| `,` | repeat it in the opposite direction |

These compose with operators, which is where they earn their keep:

- `dt)` — delete up to the closing paren
- `ct,` — change up to the next comma
- `df;` — delete through the semicolon
- `yt=` — yank everything before the `=`

**`f` vs `t` in one sentence:** use `f` when you want the character gone or
included, `t` when you want to stop short of it. `dt)` keeps the `)`; `df)`
eats it.

The `;` repeat is what makes this fast: `f,` then `;;;` walks a comma-separated
list. And `dt)` then `;` will *not* work as you expect — `.` (Level 8) is the
tool for repeating a change.

lessons.title: Jump to a character
lessons.teach: Land on the `=`.

lessons.title: Till, not onto
lessons.teach: `t(` stops one before. Land on the `s` of `process`, i.e. just before `(`.

lessons.title: Repeat with ;
lessons.teach: Walk to the third comma.
lessons.hint: `f,` then `;` twice.

lessons.title: Search backwards
lessons.teach: `F` goes left. From the end, land on the first `_`.
lessons.hint: `F_` twice. (`,` would reverse direction, not repeat it.)

lessons.title: Delete to a character
lessons.teach: `dt)` — delete the arguments but keep the parentheses.

lessons.title: Change up to a comma
lessons.teach: `ct,` — replace the first argument.

lessons.title: Delete through a character
lessons.teach: `df ` (with a space) deletes the word *and* its trailing space.

lessons.title: Yank up to a character
lessons.teach: `yt:` copies everything before the colon, `A` appends, `p` pastes it. `t` stops *before* the target, so the colon itself is not copied.
lessons.hint: `yt:` yanks `name`; `A -> ` appends; `Esc`; `p` puts.

lessons.title: f or t?
lessons.teach: Pick the right one.
lessons.question: You are on the `l` of `logger.debug(payload)` and want to delete everything from there through the dot, leaving `debug(payload)`. Which?
lessons.why: `df.` deletes *through* the `.` — inclusive. `dt.` would stop before it and leave `.debug(payload)`. `dw` stops at the `.` too (punctuation starts a new word).

links.note: `dt)` and `ci{` need brackets — AltGr combos drilled in Typing Level 9.

levels.title: Text Objects
levels.goal: Edit by structure, not by counting characters.
levels.brief:
Text objects are the second half of Vim's grammar, and the half that
actually changes how you work. Instead of *"delete four characters"* you say
*"delete the thing I am inside of"*.

The pattern is `{operator}{i|a}{object}`:

- `i` = **inner** — the contents
- `a` = **around** — the contents *plus* the delimiters or trailing space

| Object | Is |
|---|---|
| `w` `W` | word / WORD |
| `"` `'` `` ` `` | quoted string |
| `(` `)` `b` | parentheses |
| `[` `]` | square brackets |
| `{` `}` `B` | braces |
| `<` `>` | angle brackets |
| `p` | paragraph |

**The cursor does not need to be on the delimiter.** Anywhere inside works.
`ci"` from the middle of a string replaces the string. That property is what
makes text objects fast: no positioning step.

The four you will use every day: **`ciw` `ci"` `ci(` `di{`**. Learn those and
the rest follow.

lessons.title: Inner word
lessons.teach: `ciw` from anywhere in the word. The cursor is mid-word — `cw` would only change the tail.

lessons.title: Around word
lessons.teach: `daw` also eats the trailing space.

lessons.title: Inner quotes
lessons.teach: `ci"` from the middle of the string.

lessons.title: Around quotes
lessons.teach: `da'` removes the string *and* its quotes.

lessons.title: Inner parentheses
lessons.teach: `ci(` replaces the argument list.

lessons.title: Inner brackets
lessons.teach: `di[` empties a list literal — cursor inside the brackets.

lessons.title: Inner braces across lines
lessons.teach: Text objects span lines. Empty the dict body.
lessons.hint: `di{` from inside — the whole multi-line inner region goes.

lessons.title: Around parentheses
lessons.teach: `da(` takes the parens too. Turn a call into a bare name.

lessons.title: Inner paragraph
lessons.teach: `dip` deletes the block of non-blank lines around the cursor.

lessons.title: Yank a string, paste it
lessons.teach: Combine: yank the inner string, then replace the second one with it.
lessons.hint: `yi'` yanks `hola`; `j` down; `vi'` selects the other string; `p` pastes over the selection. (`ci'` then `P` does *not* work — after `Esc` the cursor sits on the quote, not inside it.)

links.note: Every bracket in these exercises is an AltGr combo on ES QWERTY.
Lists, dicts and strings — the objects you just learned to edit.

levels.title: Registers, Yank & Put
levels.brief:
Every delete is a cut. `dd` puts the line in the **unnamed register** `"`,
which is also where `x`, `c`, `s` and `y` write. That is why beginners lose
their yank: `yy` then `dd` then `p` pastes the *deleted* line.

**Putting**

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| `p` | put after cursor (charwise) / below (linewise) |
| `P` | put before cursor / above |

Whether a put is charwise or linewise depends on how the text was captured, not
on how you paste it. `yy` then `p` always makes a new line; `yiw` then `p` always
inserts inline.

**Named registers** `a`–`z`: prefix any command with `"{reg}`.

```
"ayy    yank this line into register a
"ap     put register a
"Ayy    APPEND this line to register a   (capital = append)
"_dd    delete into the black hole — does not touch any register
```

**Read-only registers worth knowing:** `"0` always holds the last *yank* (never
a delete) — so `"0p` recovers the yank you thought you lost. `"%` is the file
name, `".` the last inserted text, `"+` the system clipboard.

The classic idioms: **`yyp`** duplicate a line, **`ddp`** swap two lines,
**`xp`** swap two characters.

lessons.title: Duplicate a line
lessons.teach: `yyp` — yank the line, put it below.

lessons.title: Swap two lines
lessons.teach: `ddp` — delete the line, put it back after the next one.

lessons.title: Swap two characters
lessons.teach: `xp` — the classic typo fix.
lessons.hint: Cursor on `e`: `x` cuts it, `p` puts it after `h`.

lessons.title: Move a line far away
lessons.teach: `dd` then navigate then `p`. Move the import to the top.
lessons.hint: `dd`, `gg`, then `P` to put *above* line 1.

lessons.title: Named register
lessons.teach: Yank the first line into register `a`, then put it at the bottom without disturbing anything you delete in between.
lessons.hint: `"ayy` then `jj` then `dd` (clobbers the unnamed register, not `a`) then `"ap`.

lessons.title: The black hole register
lessons.teach: `"_dd` deletes without touching any register — your yank survives.
lessons.hint: `yy` yanks line 1; `j` `"_dd` deletes line 2 into the void; `j`? — you are now on `target`; `p` puts `keep me` below.

lessons.title: Append to a register
lessons.teach: Capital register letters append. Collect both TODO lines into `a`.
lessons.hint: `"ayy`, `jj`, `"Ayy` (append), then `"ap` puts both lines.

lessons.title: Where did my yank go?
lessons.teach: The single most common register mistake.
lessons.question: You do `yy` on line 1, then `dd` on line 5, then `p`. What gets pasted, and how do you paste what you actually wanted?
options: Line 5; use `"0p` to get the yanked line back
Line 5; the yank is gone forever
lessons.why: `dd` overwrote the unnamed register. But register `0` only ever holds the last *yank*, so `"0p` still has line 1. The habit that avoids the problem entirely: delete with `"_d` when you are about to paste.

levels.title: Undo, Repeat & the Dot Formula
levels.goal: The most valuable key in Vim is `.`
levels.brief:
`.` repeats the last **change** — not the last motion, not the last command.
A change is anything that modified the buffer: `x`, `dw`, `ciwfoo<Esc>`, `A;<Esc>`.

**The dot formula.** Structure edits so that:

> one keystroke moves to the next target, one keystroke (`.`) makes the change.

```
Goal: add a semicolon to the end of every line
  A;<Esc>      make the change on line 1
  j.           down, repeat
  j.  j.  j.   ...
```

```
Goal: rename every `old` in the file
  /old<CR>     search
  cwnew<Esc>   change the first one
  n.  n.  n.   next match, repeat
```

This beats a macro for anything under ~8 repetitions and costs nothing to set up.

**Undo**

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| `u` | undo one change |
| `Ctrl-r` | redo |
| `U` | undo all changes on the last line touched |

Undo granularity is per *Insert session*, which is another reason to press `Esc`
often: `iabc<Esc>` then `idef<Esc>` gives you two undo steps; typing `abcdef` in
one session gives you one.

lessons.title: Repeat a change
lessons.teach: Delete the first word, then repeat with `.`

lessons.title: The A; formula
lessons.teach: Add a semicolon to every line using `A;<Esc>` then `j.`

lessons.title: Dot with a text object
lessons.teach: `ciwX<Esc>` then move and `.` — the whole change repeats, including the typed text.
lessons.hint: `ciwxxx<Esc>` changes the first; `2w` to the third; `.` repeats.

lessons.title: Dot with search
lessons.teach: `/bug<CR>` `ciwfix<Esc>` `n` `.`

lessons.title: Undo and redo
lessons.teach: Delete all three lines one at a time, undo twice, redo once. You should end with one line left.
lessons.hint: Three `dd` empties the buffer; two `u` bring back `b` and `c`; one `Ctrl-r` removes `b` again.

lessons.title: Undo granularity
lessons.teach: Type `foo`, `Esc`, type `bar`, `Esc`, then a single `u`. Only `bar` should disappear.

lessons.title: What does . repeat?
lessons.teach: Be precise about this.
lessons.question: You press `dw`, then `j`, then `.`. What happens?
options: Deletes a word, moves down, moves down again
Deletes a word, moves down, deletes another word
Deletes two words on the first line
lessons.why: `.` repeats the last *change*, and `j` is a motion, not a change. So the pending change is still `dw`. This is exactly why the dot formula works: motions are free, they never disturb the repeat.

links.note: Refactoring loops into comprehensions is dot-formula work.

levels.title: Visual Modes
levels.goal: See the selection before you act on it.
levels.brief:
Visual mode inverts Vim's usual order: instead of `operator` then `motion`,
you select first and then apply.

| Key | Mode |
|---|---|
| `v` | characterwise |
| `V` | linewise |
| `Ctrl-v` | **blockwise** — rectangular |
| `gv` | reselect the last visual selection |
| `o` | jump to the other end of the selection |

In Visual mode, operators apply to the selection: `d` `c` `y` `>` `<` `u` `U`
`~` `J` `r`. Text objects work too: `vi(`, `vap`.

**When to use Visual mode:** when the extent of the edit is easier to *see* than
to *describe*. For anything you can name — a word, a string, a paragraph —
operator + text object is faster and, crucially, repeatable with `.`.

**Blockwise is the exception** — it does something no operator can:

```
Ctrl-v  jjj  I# <Esc>     comment out four lines
Ctrl-v  jjj  $A,<Esc>     append a comma to four lines
Ctrl-v  jjj  d            delete a column
```

`I` and `A` in blockwise mode insert on *every* line of the block once you press
`Esc`. That is the killer feature.

lessons.title: Characterwise select and delete
lessons.teach: `v` then a motion, then `d`.
lessons.hint: `v2e` selects `delete these`; `l` extends over the space; `d`.

lessons.title: Linewise select
lessons.teach: `V` then `j` then `d`.

lessons.title: Uppercase a selection
lessons.teach: `viwU` — select the inner word, uppercase it.

lessons.title: Reselect with gv
lessons.teach: Not everything needs gv, but know it exists. Indent, then indent again by reselecting.
lessons.hint: `Vj>` indents; `gv` reselects; `>` again.

lessons.title: Block comment
lessons.teach: `Ctrl-v` `jj` `I# ` `Esc` — comment three lines at once.

lessons.title: Block append
lessons.teach: `Ctrl-v` `jj` `$` `A,` `Esc` — add a trailing comma to each line.

lessons.title: Delete a column
lessons.teach: `Ctrl-v` `jj` `d` removes the leading `- ` bullet from each line.
lessons.hint: `<C-v>` `jj` `l` widens the block to two columns, `d`.

lessons.title: Join a selection
lessons.teach: `VjjJ` joins the selected lines into one.

lessons.title: Visual or operator?
lessons.teach: A judgement call worth getting right.
lessons.question: You need to delete the contents of a string 40 times across a file. Which approach is better?
options: `vi"d` each time — you can see what you are selecting
`di"` once, then `n.` — because `.` repeats it and Visual mode selections are not repeatable in the same way
lessons.why: Operator + text object produces a repeatable change. A visual selection followed by `d` is repeatable with `.` only over the *same size* region, which is rarely what you want. Reach for Visual mode when the region is irregular; reach for text objects when it has a name.

links.note: `Ctrl-v` and `|` chaining live on the AltGr row.

levels.title: Ex Commands & Ranges
levels.brief:
Everything after `:` operates on **lines**, addressed by a range.

**Ranges**

| Range | Means |
|---|---|
| *(none)* | the current line |
| `%` | the whole file |
| `1,10` | lines 1 to 10 |
| `.,$` | current line to end |
| `'<,'>` | the last visual selection (Vim types this for you after `V`) |
| `.,+3` | current line and the next three |

**Substitute** — `:{range}s/{pattern}/{replacement}/{flags}`

```
:s/old/new/           first match on this line
:%s/old/new/g         every match in the file
:%s/old/new/gc        ...with confirmation
:%s/\<log\>/logger/g   whole word only
:'<,'>s/^/# /         prefix the selection with #
```

Flags: `g` all matches on the line, `c` confirm, `i` ignore case, `e` no error
if not found.

**Global** — `:{range}g/{pattern}/{command}` runs an ex command on every matching
line. This is the most powerful thing in Vim, and almost nobody learns it.

```
:g/TODO/d             delete every line containing TODO
:g!/def /d            delete every line NOT containing 'def '   (also :v/def /d)
:g/^$/d               squeeze out blank lines
:g/import/normal A  # checked      run normal-mode keys on matching lines
```

**`:normal`** runs Normal-mode keystrokes over a range — the bridge between the
two languages. `:%normal A;` appends a semicolon to every line in the file.

Other essentials: `:m` move lines, `:t` (or `:co`) copy lines, `:sort`,
`:{n}` jump to line n, `:w` write, `:q` quit, `:wq`/`:x` both.

lessons.title: Substitute on one line
lessons.teach: `:s/old/new/`

lessons.title: Substitute everywhere
lessons.teach: `:%s/.../.../g` — every occurrence in the file.

lessons.title: Whole-word substitution
lessons.teach: `\<` and `\>` anchor word boundaries — without them `log` also matches inside `login`.

lessons.title: Delete matching lines
lessons.teach: `:g/pattern/d`

lessons.title: Keep only matching lines
lessons.teach: `:v/pattern/d` (inverse global) deletes everything that does *not* match.

lessons.title: Squeeze blank lines
lessons.teach: `:g/^$/d` removes every empty line.

lessons.title: Range on a selection
lessons.teach: Select two lines with `Vj`, then `:` — Vim inserts `'<,'>` for you. Comment them.

lessons.title: normal over a range
lessons.teach: `:%normal A;` runs `A;` on every line.

lessons.title: Move a line
lessons.teach: `:m0` moves the current line to the top; `:m$` to the bottom.

lessons.title: Sort a block
lessons.teach: `:%sort` — and `:sort u` also removes duplicates.

lessons.title: g plus normal
lessons.teach: The combination that replaces most macros.
lessons.question: Which command appends `  # checked` to every line containing `import`?
lessons.why: `:g/pat/normal {keys}` runs Normal-mode keystrokes on each matching line — the full power of Normal mode applied selectively. Option 1 would *replace* the word `import`; option 4 is not valid ex syntax.

levels.title: Marks, Search & Macros
levels.goal: Record once, replay a hundred times.
levels.brief:
**Marks** — `m{a-z}` sets a mark, `` `{a-z} `` jumps to it (exact position),
`'{a-z}` jumps to its line. Automatic marks worth knowing: `` `` `` is where you
were before the last jump (press it twice to bounce), `` `. `` is the last edit,
`` `^ `` is where you last left Insert mode.

**Search** — `/pattern` forward, `?pattern` backward, `n`/`N` next/previous,
`*` searches for the word under the cursor. Search is also a motion: `d/END<CR>`
deletes up to the next `END`.

**Macros** — a macro is just a register holding keystrokes.

```
qa          start recording into register a
...         do the edit, ending in a repeatable position
q           stop recording
@a          replay
10@a        replay ten times
@@          replay the last macro again
```

**Three rules for macros that don't break:**

1. **Start from a predictable position** — begin with `0` or `^`.
2. **End positioned for the next iteration** — usually with `j`.
3. **Use relative motions**, never absolute line numbers.

A macro that fails partway through simply stops (Vim aborts a count-repeated
macro on the first error), which is a feature: `100@a` on a 12-line file does
12 iterations and stops. So overshoot deliberately.

**Macro or dot?** If the repeated edit is a single change, use `.`. If it is a
*sequence* — move, edit, move, edit — record a macro.

lessons.title: Set and jump to a mark
lessons.teach: Mark the first junk line with `ma`, jump to the end, delete back to the mark. `d'a` is linewise and includes both ends.
lessons.hint: `ma` marks; `G` last line; `d'a` deletes linewise back to mark `a` — note `'a` is linewise, `` `a `` would be charwise.

lessons.title: Search as a motion
lessons.teach: `d/END<CR>` deletes from the cursor up to (not including) `END`.

lessons.title: Star search
lessons.teach: `*` jumps to the next occurrence of the word under the cursor. Change the second `total`.
lessons.hint: `*` searches for the word under the cursor and jumps to the next match — line 3.

lessons.title: Record a simple macro
lessons.teach: Record `A;<Esc>j` into register `q`, then replay it twice.
lessons.hint: `qq` start, `A;<Esc>j` the edit, `q` stop — that already did line 1. Then `2@q` for the other two.

lessons.title: A macro with structure
lessons.teach: Turn each line into a dict entry. Record: `I'` `Esc` `A': 0,` `Esc` `j`
lessons.hint: `qw` … `q` records and runs it once on line 1; `@w` does line 2.

lessons.title: Overshoot deliberately
lessons.teach: Record `I- <Esc>j`, then replay it **50** times on a 4-line buffer. The macro aborts by itself when `j` fails on the last line, so over-counting is free — you never need to know how many lines there are.
lessons.hint: `qa` `I- ` `Esc` `j` `q` records and already runs iteration 1; `50@a` does the rest and stops on the error.

lessons.title: Recursive-style repeat
lessons.teach: Apply the same change down a file with `@@`.
lessons.hint: `qz…q` runs once, `@z` again, then `@@` twice. `@@` replays whichever macro you ran last, so you stop having to name the register.

lessons.title: Why did my macro break?
lessons.teach: The most common macro bug.
lessons.question: You record a macro that starts by pressing `w` to get to the second word. It works on line 1 and mangles line 4. Most likely cause?
options: Line 4 has different structure, so `w` lands somewhere else — the macro used a fragile motion instead of an anchored one
You need to re-record after every line
lessons.why: Macros are literal keystroke replays with no awareness of content. Anchor them: start with `0` or `^`, and prefer `f{char}` or `/pattern` over counting words, so the motion adapts to each line.

levels.title: Neovim in Practice
levels.goal: Config, LSP, buffers and windows. Making it yours.
levels.brief:
You now know Vim. This level is about **Neovim** specifically — the parts
that are not in vi.

**Buffers, windows, tabs** — three different things, and confusing them is the
usual source of pain.

- A **buffer** is a file loaded in memory. `:ls` lists them, `:b {name}` switches,
  `:bd` closes.
- A **window** is a viewport onto a buffer. `:split` / `:vsplit`,
  `Ctrl-w h/j/k/l` to move between them, `Ctrl-w q` to close.
- A **tab** is a layout of windows. Most people who want tabs actually want
  buffers.

**Configuration is Lua.** `~/.config/nvim/init.lua`:

```lua
vim.opt.number = true            -- :set number
vim.opt.relativenumber = true    -- motions become countable at a glance
vim.opt.expandtab = true
vim.opt.shiftwidth = 4
vim.g.mapleader = ' '            -- set BEFORE loading plugins

vim.keymap.set('n', '<leader>w', '<cmd>write<cr>', { desc = 'Save' })
vim.keymap.set('n', '<esc>', '<cmd>nohlsearch<cr>')
vim.keymap.set('v', '<', '<gv')  -- keep the selection after indenting
```

`relativenumber` deserves a special mention: it turns "delete the next six
lines" from counting into reading. It is the single highest-value option in the
list.

**LSP** — Neovim speaks the Language Server Protocol natively. With a Python
server (`pyright` or `ruff` + `basedpyright`) attached you get, in Normal mode:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| `gd` | go to definition |
| `gr` | list references |
| `K` | hover documentation |
| `<leader>rn` | rename symbol across the project |
| `<leader>ca` | code action (quick fix) |
| `[d` `]d` | previous / next diagnostic |

`<leader>rn` is worth the whole setup on its own: a semantic rename beats
`:%s/old/new/g` because it will not touch a string that happens to contain the
same characters.

**Plugin manager** — `lazy.nvim` is the current default. A minimal, real
`init.lua` is about 40 lines and gives you fuzzy finding (telescope), treesitter
highlighting, and LSP.

**How to keep improving:** `:help {topic}` is genuinely excellent — `:help
text-objects`, `:help :g`, `:help registers`. And `:checkhealth` when something
is broken.

lessons.title: Edit your options
lessons.teach: Add `relativenumber` below `number` in a config file.
lessons.hint: `yyp` duplicates the line but leaves the cursor in column 0, so `ciw` there would change `vim`. Press `fn` first, to land on `number`.

lessons.title: Add a keymap
lessons.teach: Append a leader mapping after the existing one.
lessons.hint: `yyp` duplicates; `f>` lands on the `>` of `<leader>`, `l` steps onto the `w`, `rq` replaces it; then `:s/write/quit/` for the command.

lessons.title: Fix a Lua table
lessons.teach: Turn the single-line table into the idiomatic multi-line form by replacing the contents.

lines: local opts = { noremap = true, silent = true }

lessons.title: Comment out a plugin
lessons.teach: Block-comment three lines of a lazy.nvim spec with `Ctrl-v`.

lessons.title: Refactor with :normal
lessons.teach: Convert every `vim.opt.X = true` line to `vim.opt.X = false` with one ex command.

lessons.title: Buffers vs windows
lessons.teach: Get the mental model right.
lessons.question: You have three files open and want to see two of them side by side. What do you actually need?
options: Two windows showing two of the three buffers
Two buffers — the third must be closed
lessons.why: Buffers are the files; windows are the viewports. Three buffers can coexist with any number of windows, including one. `:vsplit` then `:b {other}` gives you the side-by-side view without closing anything.

lessons.title: Rename correctly
lessons.teach: The last habit to build.
lessons.question: You need to rename the function `load` to `load_config` across a Python project. Which is safest?
options: Manual search and replace with confirmation
lessons.why: An LSP rename understands scope: it will not rename a *different* `load` in another class, nor a `load` inside a string or comment. The regex options either over-match (option 1 hits `download`) or cannot distinguish two unrelated symbols with the same name.

links.note: Typing Level 11 drills Lua config syntax.
Tooling and packaging — the Python side of the same workflow.
